Yale Health Navigator

Describe your situation in plain words and get the Yale Health line to call, a plan for the call, and a coverage check that quotes the rules.

Student: Shirley Xu  |  Course: AI Foundations for Managers (MGT 409), final project
GitHub repo (public, clone this): https://github.com/shirleyxu414-sys/yale-health-navigator
Clone: git clone https://github.com/shirleyxu414-sys/yale-health-navigator.git
App link: not online. It runs locally from a fresh clone by following the README (about five minutes), at http://127.0.0.1:8000.

1. Title and links

Yale Health Navigator is a web app for Yale students, staff and faculty, dependents and visiting students: type a situation such as "lower back pain for weeks, I want physical therapy", and it tells you which Yale Health line to call, what to bring up on the call, and what your plan covers, with every coverage claim quoted from a Yale Health document and anything it cannot verify sent to Member Services at (203) 432-0246.

Repository (public): https://github.com/shirleyxu414-sys/yale-health-navigator. The README explains how to run it. It needs Python 3.10 or newer and one key, PORTKEY_API_KEY, in a .env file in the repo folder or the folder above it. The only model is gpt-6-luna, through Portkey.

2. Motivation

Who has the problem. Every Yale member who needs care and does not know where to start. Yale Health is one organization with several doors: Member Services for coverage and referrals, Acute Care for same-day needs, the primary care team, Physical Therapy and Sports Medicine (PTSMC), mental health, and more, each with its own phone number and hours. The rules differ by who you are: a student has Basic Coverage and a separate hospitalization and specialty plan that can be waived; staff and faculty follow an employee booklet; dependents and visiting students have their own terms.

How they handle it today. They search the Yale Health website, open the Member Booklet or the Student Guide (the Student Guide alone runs past 110 pages), or call Member Services, which is open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. A first-time question like "can I get physical therapy for my back?" really involves four answers spread over different pages: which line to call (the main line, not PTSMC directly), that a PCP referral is required first, that physical therapy is covered at 100% only with that referral, and that students who waived the hospitalization and specialty plan are not eligible.

What it costs. Time and frustration, and sometimes the wrong first call: calling the wrong line, arriving without a referral, or assuming something is covered when it is not. I did not measure this with a survey. The evidence I can offer is the structure of the documents themselves: the answer to one ordinary question sits on at least four different pages and two PDFs, and the phone line that can confirm it is closed evenings and weekends.

3. What is new here

The alternatives I compared against.

AlternativeWhat it does wellWhere it falls short for this problem
Yale Health website and the Member Booklet / Student Guide PDFsAuthoritative and completeYou must already know which page and which role applies; answers are spread across pages and PDFs
Member Services phone line, (203) 432-0246A person who can confirm anythingOpen Monday to Friday, 8:30 to 5:00; you wait, and you call before you know what to ask
MyChart messagesGood for non-urgent care team questionsReplies take about two business days; not for appointments or anything urgent
A general chatbot such as ChatGPTInstant, friendly, understands plain wordsAnswers from memory: it can state coverage or phone numbers that are wrong, and nothing makes it cite a Yale document

What this project does differently.

  • Role-aware, rule-file grounded. Each role has its own rule file (plus one shared file). A role only ever sees its own file and the common file, so a visiting student is never answered from student rules.
  • Every claim is checked in code. The coverage agent must copy one sentence word for word from a rule it cites. Code then checks that the sentence is in that rule and that every number in the answer is too. If not, the person sees "I don't know, ask Yale Health. Member Services: (203) 432-0246."
  • It routes before it explains. The first output is the line to call, with an open-now badge from the hours in the rule files, then a plan with the few things a person would not know to bring up (for example, ask for the PT referral, because PT is covered 100% only with one).
  • The referral problem has its own tools, built from Yale Health's referral lists and with no list of doctors: a "Do I need a referral?" checker, a four-stage referral tracker and a "Your PCP" card.
  • Safety is in code, not just in the prompt: emergencies, prompt injection and "what do I have?" are handled before any model call.

Why it matters, and the honest part. This is not a new model or a new medical technique; the idea is to put a careful grounding layer between a language model and a confusing but high-stakes set of rules. It does not replace Member Services, it is not a coverage decision, and it only knows what is in the rule files I built by hand from public Yale pages. Yale Health could build something similar with access to live eligibility data, which would beat this app on accuracy for individual members.

4. The agents

The agents and their tools

AgentWhat it doesTools
Router (model)Reads the situation and decides: category (routine, urgent), the line to call, what the person wants, whether they already have a referral, and the timing if they said itNone. One call
Coverage checker (model)Given the category and what the person wants, reads only the role file and common file and answers: is it covered, what condition applies, what is excluded. Must quote one rule sentence per claimNone. One call. The rule text is placed in the prompt
Plan builder (model)Builds the timeline, the "do not forget to mention" points, the write-down list and the checklist. Never writes a script. A coverage-only question gets no timelineNone. One call
Chat agent (model)Answers follow-up questions as a message thread, with the plan's context carried inlookup_rules: keyword search over the role file plus the common file, returns at most 4 rules. At most 4 rounds, each one checked against the budget
Code, not modelsScreen (emergency, crisis, injection, diagnosis); verifier and grounding check; referral checker; glossary; open-now badges; calendar file; Print and Copy call sheetPlain Python and JavaScript. Zero tokens

How they are organized

The first three agents form a fixed pipeline, with handoffs in code: the screen runs first; the router's output (category, line, wants) goes to the coverage checker; the coverage result, after the verifier, goes to the plan builder; the page draws all of it. Handing work through code instead of letting agents call each other keeps each call small and makes every step loggable. The chat agent is separate: it uses a tool loop instead of a fixed pipeline because a follow-up question can be about anything.

Models used and why

gpt-6-luna only, through Portkey with the OpenAI client. It is the course model, and it fits the job: the task is short structured JSON output over a small rule set, not open-ended reasoning, so a low-cost model is enough and keeps a plan at a fraction of a cent (section 5). The model name lives in one place, backend/config.py, and a test fails if any other model name appears anywhere in the repo.

Grounding design: one example trace

The chat agent's real trace for "Is dental covered?" (student role) from the audit log, output/audit_trail.json:

screen            passed
diagnosis_check   passed
route             a question: answered by the bot
lookup_tool       1 lookup; rules seen: common.dental, common.referral_other,
                  student.hospitalization_specialty, student.pt_requires_hospitalization_specialty
verifier          1 passed citation, grounding, number and no-diagnosis checks; 0 did not
outcome           answer, rule cited: common.dental        tokens used: 1,967

claim (quoted from the rule): "Yale Health does not offer dental insurance for adults."
source on the rule:           Yale OISS Dental & Vision Care page; Yale Health Student Guide
                              2025-2026, Pediatric Dental Care section; gradprofdenteye.yale.edu

Had the model written a claim that is not in common.dental, or a price that is not in it, the verifier would have replaced the answer with "I don't know, ask Yale Health." and logged a grounding failure. The rule contains no premium or copay numbers on purpose: they change every year, so the rule points to the plan page instead.

Cost uses the published rates for gpt-6-luna reported by third-party pricing pages: $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.01 per million cached input tokens, $0.50 per million output tokens (eesel.ai, anotherwrapper.com). I did not find the provider's own page, so these are second-hand rates; if the course rate differs, the cost scales linearly. The API reported zero cached tokens on every call.

Cost per user per month, and at scale

Assumption (mine, not measured): a member uses the app for 4 plans and 10 chat questions in a month; referral checks and everything else in code are free.

ScaleHow it is computedMonthly cost
Per user4 x $0.00165 + 10 x $0.00041about $0.011
100 users100 x $0.0107about $1.07
10,000 users10,000 x $0.0107about $107

For scale, about $107 a month is the model cost for a campus-sized population of 10,000 users under that usage assumption; hosting and staff time are not included. A plan costs about a sixth of a cent, so the per-session cap of 200,000 input tokens is roughly 26 plans and the per-address cap of 1,000,000 is roughly 130, which is a backstop against runaway use, not a limit a normal person reaches.

Cost-cutting steps, and whether they hurt performance

StepEffectDid it hurt? Evidence
Do everything possible in code: referral checker, emergency and crisis screen, injection and diagnosis refusal, glossary, open-now badges, calendar, call sheetZero tokens for those paths; an emergency never waits on a modelNo. These are deterministic and covered by tests (495 pass)
Chat uses a lookup tool that returns at most 4 rules, instead of putting a whole rule file in the promptA chat question costs 1,956 input tokens on average. The student and common files together are about 7,200 tokens (estimated at 4 characters per token), so sending them every turn would roughly quadruple the inputPartly. "Is dental covered?" and "Do I need prior authorization?" answered correctly. But "Where is the official coverage page?" failed ("I don't know") because the lookup returns rule text, not URLs. I fixed that one question with a code path rather than widening the lookup
One call per agent, no loops in the pipeline; plan limited to a few points; at most 4 coverage topics3 calls per plan, about 8 to 12 secondsNo evidence of harm
Token budget guard: per-session and per-address caps, checked before every call, including each round of the chat tool loopCaps the worst caseNo. The Safety demo shows it stopping a run before the model call
Strict grounding check (quote and every number must be in the cited rule)Prevents wrong answersYes, a cost to quality. In a live test the model wrote "$0" for "covered at 100%". The check treated "$0" as a number not in the rule and replaced a correct answer with "I don't know". It happened on repeated runs one day and passed on later runs. Safe, but it can look like a false refusal
Prompt cachingNot realized: the API reported 0 cached tokens on all 5 measured runsUntested. Each call repeats a fixed instruction block, so caching is the obvious next saving. If a third of a plan's input became cached at $0.01 per million, a plan would cost about 14% less. That figure is an illustration, not a measurement

6. Safety

The risks that matter for this app, and what stops each one:

RiskWhat I built
Emergency: someone describes chest pain or a crisis to a chatbot and receives a planAn emergency and crisis screen in code, before any model call: the person sees only "Call 911 or go to the emergency room now.", the nearby ERs, Acute Care and the Referrals line, or the 988 crisis line. No plan, no coverage talk
Diagnosis or treatment advice"What do I have?" and "Is this serious?" are refused in code ("I can't diagnose, that's for a clinician. Here's who to call:"). Every model output is also scanned for diagnosis and treatment words. Symptoms get a "get emergency help right away if" list from the rule files, never a condition name
Prompt injectionEverything typed is data. "Ignore your rules", "you are now a doctor" and fake system messages are refused in code before the model. Model output is checked again on the way out
Invented facts (wrong coverage, made-up phone numbers or prices)The quote-and-numbers grounding check; phone numbers are scrubbed unless they are in the rule files; anything unverified becomes "I don't know" with Member Services' number. A role never sees another role's rules
Overspending and runaway loopsA per-session cap (200,000 input tokens) and a per-address cap (1,000,000), checked before every model call, including each round of the chat's tool loop, which is itself limited to 4 rounds
Health privacyNo login, no cookies, no localStorage. What a person types lives in the page only and is gone on refresh. The server keeps a metadata log and an audit log for graders; they are local files, never committed

Defenses working

The app has a Safety demo page (/safety-demo) that runs the defenses live with no model and no tokens. Figure 7 is a real capture: 5 of 5 injection attempts refused, 3 of 3 diagnosis requests refused, 2 of 3 grounding cases replaced (the third was valid and shown), and the budget guard stopping a run before the model call.

Tests. The suite has 495 tests, all passing on 26 October 2026: python -m pytest tests. Safety coverage includes tests/injection_test.py (every injection attempt refused), the grounding and budget tests in tests/test_defenses.py, and the repo-wide checks that only gpt-6-luna appears and no key is committed. Four live tests call the real model and are skipped when no key is present.

What I expect, and have not proven: fewer wrong first calls, fewer visits that start without a referral, and shorter calls to Member Services because the person arrives with the right question. How I would test it: five to ten Yale members each try three real situations; I would time how long it takes them to find the right line and the referral rule with and without the app, and record whether they would have called the right place first.

8. Limits and next steps

What does not work yet

  • No real-user test (section 7), so the impact is argued, not measured.
  • Thin rule files for some roles. The student file has 13 rules and the staff and faculty file 8, plus 17 shared ones. Dependents and visiting students have one role-specific rule each, so most of their questions fall back to Member Services. Rules were written by hand from public Yale pages and can go out of date; one rule (the Aetna switch after three years) comes from a Yale benefits page rather than the booklet and applies to a subset of staff, and the app says so.
  • Safe but sometimes over-strict. The grounding check can replace a correct answer with "I don't know" when the model rephrases a number, as the "$0" case showed.
  • No personal eligibility. It cannot know a member's actual plan, whether they waived coverage, or whether a referral was approved. It always says to confirm with Member Services.
  • Not hosted. It runs locally from the repo; there is no public link. Prompt caching is not used yet (0 cached tokens measured).
  • The chat can answer only what the keyword lookup finds; a question phrased with words that are not in the rules may be answered with "I don't know" even when a rule exists.

What I would build next

  1. Run the five-to-ten-person user test above and publish the times and quotes.
  2. Host the app so a grader or a member can open a link, with the budget caps already in place.
  3. Add more rules for dependents and visiting students, each with its source page, and a yearly review so stale rules are caught.
  4. Turn on prompt caching for the fixed instruction block and re-measure cost.
  5. Accept equivalent number formats in the grounding check ("covered at 100%" and "$0"), with tests, to remove the false refusals without weakening the rule.
  6. Ask Yale Health to review the rule files; a live connection to eligibility would make the answers personal.
